question: A TV channel showed this before the Bush tax cuts ran out. The top rate looks set to explode. Where's the trick?
answer: In the axis, which starts at 34%. So the 35% bar is one point tall and the 39.6% bar five and a half. Drawn from zero, the second bar is only 13% taller: a real rise of 4.6 points, not a quintupling. A bar is read by its length, and a length means something only from zero.
move: Before you read a bar chart, find where its axis starts.

scene.headline: If Bush tax cuts expire
scene.label: Top income tax rate
scene.ask: Tap the part that's fooling you
scene.found: Yes: the axis starts at 34%, not at zero.
scene.miss: That part tells the truth. Look at what the bottom of the bars stands for.

misses.marks: The numbers on the bars are right. It's their heights that lie. Why?
misses.headline: The headline only says what changes. The drawing does the shouting.

scene.name: The cut-off axis
scene.lesson: A bar's length only means something from zero. Cut the bottom off and 13% looks like 460%.

source: Media Matters for America, "A history of dishonest Fox charts" (2012); IRS top marginal rates, 2012 and 2013

question: Around 2013 this chart went round: global warming stopped in 1998. The line really is flat. Where's the trick?
answer: In the years. 1998 was a record El Niño spike, so a chart that starts there starts on a peak and finds the next years flat. Open the window and the same NASA readings climb about 0.9°C from 1980 to 2023; every year since 2014 beat 1998. Where a series starts and stops can make it say almost anything.
move: When a chart covers a few years, ask why those years.

scene.headline: Global warming stopped in 1998
scene.label: World temperature vs 1951–80
scene.found: Yes: it starts on 1998, a record spike.
scene.miss: That part is honest. Ask why the chart begins and ends where it does.

misses.yaxis: The scale is a fair one for these years. The question is which years.
misses.marks: Those are NASA's real readings. What's missing is the years around them.

scene.name: The cherry-picked window
scene.lesson: Start a series on a peak and anything looks flat. Always ask what came before and after.

source: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies, GISTEMP v4, global annual mean surface temperature

question: India now emits more carbon dioxide than Russia, Japan or Germany, and this chart makes it look like the villain. Where's the trick?
answer: In what is counted: totals for whole countries. India has 1.4 billion people, ten times Russia and seventeen times Germany. Per person, an Indian emits about 2.1 tonnes a year: a sixth of a Russian, under a third of a German or a Japanese. Comparing totals between countries of such different sizes mostly compares their populations.
move: Before comparing totals, divide by the people behind them.

scene.headline: India out-pollutes Russia, Japan and Germany
scene.honest: Per person, India emits the least by far
scene.label: CO₂ emitted in 2023, billion t
scene.found: Yes: these are totals for countries of very different sizes.
scene.miss: The figures are right. Read what they count, one line above the bars.

misses.yaxis: The axis starts at zero, so the bars are fair lengths. Of what, though?
misses.headline: True, in total. But a total is the wrong yardstick here. Why?

scene.name: Totals, not per person
scene.lesson: A big country tops every total. Divide by the people before you compare.

source: Global Carbon Budget 2024 (Friedlingstein et al.) and UN World Population Prospects 2024, via Our World in Data
